units.text: 2. A History of Those Who Must Answer
From Action to Character, from Character to Relationship

Imagine a hearing in which everyone agrees on the facts but nobody agrees on the question. One participant asks what the person did. Another asks what kind of person they became. A third asks which role they betrayed. A fourth wants to know what consequences they could foresee. The history of responsibility is not merely a succession of answers to the same question. It also involves changes in which question is considered decisive.

There is no single genealogy in which humanity departed from superstition and proceeded in an orderly way to the modern rational individual. Different traditions have combined intention, consequence, relationship, law, and character. Disputes have existed within the same tradition. We will follow several conceptual turning points without turning their selection into a complete history of the world, and without assuming that our vocabulary was already that of ancient authors.

In Book III of the Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle examines voluntary actions, coercion, and ignorance. The difficult cases are “mixed”: the person who throws cargo overboard to save the ship makes a choice, but in circumstances they would not have wished for. The analysis does not allow every act to be reduced to free choice or the complete absence of choice. It calls for examining particular circumstances and what the agent knew. [ 5 ]

This observation remains fruitful. A worker accepts a risky task to avoid losing income. Nobody physically pushes them into it, but neither are they choosing from a menu of equal possibilities. We can acknowledge the choice without idealizing its freedom. We can criticize conduct without pretending that its author had the same power as the person who imposed the conditions. This middle ground is precisely what discussions of merit often erase.

Virtue ethics also shifts attention toward the formation of the person. An action does not come from nothing: habits, ways of noticing, and practical judgment contribute to it. In the Aristotelian tradition, practical wisdom does not mean instrumental skill alone. Someone can calculate very well how to achieve a bad end. Understanding what is worth pursuing is part of the problem. Yet virtue ethics is not alone in valuing character, just as rule-based ethics does not automatically ignore consequences. [ 6 ]

From this perspective, a society concerned with responsibility cannot regard education as simply transmitting prohibitions. It must ask what kinds of people its rewards produce. If it admires success regardless of the means, it cannot be sincerely surprised when concern for the means weakens. This is a normative criticism of its consistency, not a psychological law according to which every person will copy rewarded behavior.

In the Confucian tradition, moral life is closely connected with relationships, cultivation, and roles. The idea should not be reduced to mechanical obedience. A ruler’s conduct and moral example matter, and relationships involve expectations of several parties, even if they are not organized according to contemporary egalitarianism. A role describes not only what you may ask of others but also what you must become to fulfill it properly. [ 7 ]

Mencius uses the case of a child at risk of falling into a well to discuss spontaneous compassion. He also connects good government with the material conditions under which people can cultivate a moral life. In ancient Chinese debate, this differentiated concern for those close to us encountered the challenge of impartial concern associated with Mozi. We therefore have no single “Eastern mentality,” but a dispute about the relationship between affection, order, and obligations toward strangers. [ 8 ]

The dispute still concerns us. A parent who favors their child at their own table is not doing the same thing as an official who favors that child in a public selection process. A relationship can create a special duty in one context and a conflict of interest in another. History offers more than ornamental wisdom here: it forces us to acknowledge that the same apparent virtue, loyalty, can protect a vulnerable being or defend an injustice.
Duty Before a Visible or Invisible Judge

People have also located accountability beyond immediately visible relationships. If actions have moral consequences within a cosmic order, escaping the community’s sanctions does not close the case. This idea can limit the powerful person’s arbitrariness: winning does not automatically mean being right. But it can also encourage the interpretation of misfortune as deserved punishment. The two uses must be separated, even when expressed in the same religious vocabulary.

In Indian Buddhist traditions, intention plays a central role in assessing action and understanding karma. These traditions connect moral practice with reducing suffering and transforming mental dispositions. They cannot be compressed into the slogan that every suffering person has received exactly what they deserve. The doctrines, interpretations, and their relationship to compassion are more complex than a popular accounting of cosmic rewards. [ 9 ]

We can independently formulate a test for any religious explanation of suffering. If the explanation makes me more attentive to what I can repair, it has a certain moral function. If it authorizes me to refuse help because I assume the victim is guilty in some invisible history, it requires an extremely strong justification. It is not enough that the explanation cannot be disproved. The very inaccessibility of the evidence should prevent us from using it as a verdict on another person’s life.

Belief in God as judge does not produce a single conception of responsibility either. We can conceive of obedience to a command, accountability for intention, fidelity to a covenant, or the obligation to care for the vulnerable. We can also conceive of the protest of someone who suffers without acknowledging the guilt attributed to them. The Book of Job, to which we will return, makes it impossible to reduce all religious reflection to the formula “you suffered, therefore you deserved it.” [ 10 ]

The tension between imposed law and justifiable law reappears in another form in Kant. Moral autonomy does not mean doing whatever you wish, but considering yourself bound by principles you can rationally uphold, not merely by your immediate interests. The formula of humanity requires that we not treat a person merely as a means. Universalization asks whether the rule by which we act can also be upheld when it does not benefit us. These ideas do not automatically turn every dilemma into a simple calculation. [ 11 ]

Think of an employer who says he can conceal a risk because workers need their wages. He uses their very vulnerability as an instrument for securing acceptance. A perspective centered on respect for persons asks whether consent can still perform its purported moral function when important information is deliberately withheld. The signed contract does not exhaust the issue. Sometimes the paper records an agreement; at other times, it certifies an asymmetry that the signature does not heal.

John Stuart Mill’s utilitarianism places the well-being of those affected at the center of assessment, rather than the prestige of the decision-maker’s intentions. Happiness and suffering do not become relevant only when they belong to the agent. Mill also discusses justice, rules, and motivation; he does not propose simply satisfying every impulse that produces immediate pleasure. Nevertheless, the orientation toward consequences leaves open the difficult question of sacrificing some for the benefit of others. [ 12 ]

We should not hastily choose here between two caricatures: the rigid person who follows the rule and lets the world burn, and the accountant who justifies every cruelty with a convenient total. The rule protects precisely because it cannot be suspended for every local advantage. The consequence matters precisely because the victim is not saved by the purity of our intention. Mature judgment must bear this tension rather than replace it with a slogan about good intentions or good results.
When the World Becomes Too Large for a Single Conscience

In a small community, you can see the person affected by your gesture. In a large organization, you see a task, an indicator, a stage. The person affected may appear much later, in another place, in another department. This distance must not be confused with the absence of a connection. Sometimes the division of labor distributes expertise; at other times, it also distributes the possibility of no longer seeing the overall result.

Durkheim analyzed solidarity based on similarity and the solidarity of a differentiated society in which people depend on one another’s functions. For him, the division of labor was not merely a matter of economic efficiency but also a problem of integration and moral regulation. His analysis does not oblige us to approve every existing order. It helps us notice that an individual’s everyday autonomy may depend on a social network they never encounter in its entirety. [ 13 ]

The interpretation proposed here is this: the more indirect dependence becomes, the more explicit the means of seeing obligations must be. We cannot rely solely on the emotion of an encounter. Someone inspecting a facility may never know the people protected by their work. That does not diminish the inspection’s value. A responsible society must make contributions that prevent harm without producing a heroic story both intelligible and worthy of reward.

In his 1919 lecture on politics, Max Weber placed the ethic of conviction and the ethic of responsibility in tension. One emphasizes fidelity to commitment, the other acceptance of an action’s foreseeable consequences. The distinction should be read neither as a license for cynicism nor as an obligation to abandon every principle. The problem is how someone can act in the world without hiding their effects behind inner purity. [ 14 ]

A leader who announces a generous reform but refuses to examine its implementation does not demonstrate generosity by ignoring failure. Conversely, a leader who continually justifies injustice through “realism” does not demonstrate responsibility merely by counting constraints. Conviction needs to confront the world; the analysis of consequences needs moral limits. Without the first correction, idealism can become indifference to effects. Without the second, pragmatism can become a technique of efficient domination.

Nietzsche challenged the presentation of guilt and punishment as transparent expressions of an obvious moral order. His genealogy investigates the relationships between morality, power, debt, and the formation of conscience. It does not follow that every moral criticism is false or that vulnerable people do not matter. What follows is an uncomfortable question for any institution distributing blame: whose interests are served by the precise way it has defined it? [ 15 ]

Ethics of care brought dependence and the work needed to sustain life to the fore. Carol Gilligan, Nel Noddings, Eva Feder Kittay, and Joan Tronto contributed in different ways to this shift in emphasis. Care is neither a feminine biological essence nor the abandonment of justice. One of its political questions is who provides care, under what conditions, and who can afford to appear independent because someone else takes care of their needs. [ 16 ]

Through this lens, the image of the self-sufficient adult changes. Someone who devotes their life to ideas may depend on another person who cooks, cleans, cares for a child, or accompanies an ill parent. If we call the first activity a vocation and the second merely a natural obligation, we have already distributed prestige and burden. Responsibility concerns more than who did wrong. It also concerns who maintains the conditions under which others can succeed.

Technological power adds a problem the book will follow to the end: effects can extend beyond their authors’ lifetimes. We need not assume that we can control the future to recognize that we can narrow the options of those who will inhabit it. The history of responsibility thus remains open. It moves from the question “what will happen to me because of what I did?” to the question “what might happen to others because we can do so much?”
